tips.title: Keep the article after an opinion verb
tips.body: After *aimer*, *adorer*, *détester* and *préférer*, a noun keeps its **le / la / les**: *j'aime **le** sport, je déteste **les** légumes*. English drops the article — *I like sport* — so this is the one to watch, and it is checked in almost every writing task.

tips.title: Verb after verb means infinitive
tips.body: When an opinion verb is followed by another verb, the second one stays in the **infinitive**: *j'aime **jouer**, je déteste **faire** mes devoirs*. Only the first verb changes for the person. One conjugated verb, then the dictionary form.

tips.title: Parce que does not need a comma but does need a verb
tips.body: *Parce que* introduces a **clause**, so it must be followed by a subject and a verb: *parce que **c'est** amusant*, not *parce que amusant*. Before a vowel it becomes **parce qu'**: *parce qu'il est génial*.

tips.title: Ne … pas goes round the conjugated verb
tips.body: *Je n'aime **pas** le sport. Je n'aime **pas** jouer.* The negative wraps the first verb only. An infinitive after it is untouched, and *ne* becomes *n'* before a vowel.

tips.title: Trop, assez and vraiment lift an opinion
tips.body: *C'est **trop** difficile. C'est **assez** intéressant. C'est **vraiment** génial.* One intensifier before the adjective turns a bare opinion into a graded one, which is what **range** means on the mark scheme.

why.matters: Every speaking and writing task in the GCSE asks what you think, and an opinion with no reason scores almost nothing. This topic is the machinery for the rest of the course: a ladder of verbs from *j'adore* to *je déteste*, the article French keeps after them where English drops it, the infinitive that follows when the thing you like is a verb, and *parce que* with a real clause behind it. Learn the shape once and every topic that follows, from school to holidays to the environment, is a matter of changing the noun.

examples.title: Rating a film with a friend
examples.body: Two friends leaving a cinema run the whole ladder in a minute: one adored it, the other thought it was all right, a third hated it. The French ladder has five rungs and they all take the same grammar, so the only decision is how strong you feel. Then comes the word that turns a rating into an opinion: *parce que*, followed by a full clause with a verb in it. *J'ai adoré parce que c'était drôle* earns; *j'ai adoré* alone is a shrug.

examples.title: The article English drops
examples.body: English says *I like sport*; French will not let you. After an opinion verb the noun keeps its article, and it is always the definite one: *j'aime le sport, j'adore la musique, je déteste les devoirs*. Dropping it is the commonest Year 9 error in writing, and it is an English habit rather than a French mistake. If the thing you like is an action instead, the second verb stays in the infinitive: *j'aime jouer*, never *j'aime je joue*.

rows: the definite one, never du or un

examples.title: The reason that earns the mark
examples.body: A mark scheme pays for opinions that are justified, and a justified opinion has four parts that can be assembled in any topic: the verb from the ladder, the thing with its article or its infinitive, an adjective graded with *très* or *trop* or *assez*, and a reason introduced by *parce que* with a verb in it. Add *par contre* and a second opinion, and you have the balanced answer the top band wants, built from parts you can reuse for ever.

steps.title: Saying what you like
steps.body:
Every French opinion question can be answered with a small ladder of verbs, from strongest liking to strongest disliking.

**j'adore** → **j'aime beaucoup** → **j'aime** → **je n'aime pas** → **je déteste**

They all work the same way, and the thing you have an opinion about follows straight after — either a **noun** or a **verb**.

**With a noun, the article stays.** *J'aime **le** sport. J'adore **la** musique. Je déteste **les** devoirs.* English says *I like sport* with no article; French never drops it after these verbs. This is the single most common error in Year 9 writing.

**With a verb, the second verb is an infinitive.** *J'aime **jouer** au foot. Je déteste **faire** mes devoirs.* The first verb is conjugated for the person; the second is the dictionary form and never changes.

**Préférer** works the same way and adds a comparison: *je préfère le tennis*, or *je préfère regarder la télé*.

The verb **aimer** is regular **-er**, so it is worth having in full: its pattern is the pattern of most French verbs.

visuals.alt: A conjugation table for aimer in the present tense, showing the stem and ending for each person

steps.title: Saying why
steps.body: An opinion on its own scores little. **Parce que** and a reason is what turns it into an answer. **Parce que** means *because* and must be followed by a **subject and a verb** — a full clause. The reason is almost always **c'est** + an adjective: *parce que **c'est** amusant / intéressant / difficile / ennuyeux*. Before a vowel, **que** becomes **qu'**: *parce qu'**il** est génial, parce qu'**on** peut…* **Adjectives for reasons**, in pairs: - *amusant / ennuyeux* — fun / boring - *facile / difficile* — easy / hard - *intéressant / nul* — interesting / rubbish - *génial / horrible* — great / awful - *passionnant / fatigant* — exciting / tiring **Intensifiers** grade them: *très, trop, assez, vraiment*. *C'est **trop** difficile* is not the same as *c'est **assez** difficile*, and using both in one answer shows control. **Negatives** wrap the conjugated verb: *je n'aime **pas** le sport parce que c'est fatigant*. Note that after a negative, *le* stays *le* — the article does not change after *aimer* the way it does after *avoir*.

visuals.fallback: Donner une raison: parce que — because; c'est — it is; amusant — fun; ennuyeux — boring; facile — easy; difficile — hard, difficult; intéressant — interesting; nul — rubbish; génial — great; passionnant — exciting; fatigant — tiring; très — very; trop — too; assez — quite; vraiment — really

steps.title: Asking and answering
steps.body:
Opinion questions come in three shapes, and each has a matching answer.

**Tu aimes … ?** — *Do you like …?* Answer with the ladder: *Oui, j'aime beaucoup … / Non, je n'aime pas …*

**Qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire ?** — *What do you like doing?* Answer with an **infinitive**: *J'aime **écouter** de la musique.*

**Qu'est-ce que tu préfères, X ou Y ?** — *Which do you prefer?* Answer with **je préfère** and, for a top mark, the reason: *Je préfère le cinéma parce que c'est plus intéressant.*

**Two things a speaking examiner listens for.** First, that you **answer the question asked** — an infinitive to *aimes faire*, a noun to *tu aimes*. Second, that you **develop**: opinion, reason, and one more sentence. *J'aime le foot* is a mark; *j'aime le foot parce que c'est passionnant, et je joue tous les samedis* is the top of the band.

**Agreeing and disagreeing** with someone else's opinion is worth having too: *moi aussi* (me too), *moi non plus* (me neither), *pas moi* (not me), *je suis d'accord* (I agree), *je ne suis pas d'accord* (I disagree).

Tu préfères le foot ou le tennis ?

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Write the five opinion verbs from strongest liking to strongest disliking.
2. Translate: *I hate homework.* Keep the article.
3. Translate: *I like listening to music.*

**Part B.**

4. Give an opinion on French, with a reason using *parce que*.
5. Write *I don't like sport* in French, with the negative in the right place.
6. Write the present tense of **aimer** in full.

**Part C.**

7. Write two contrasting opinions joined by *par contre*, each with a reason.
8. Answer *Qu'est-ce que tu préfères, le cinéma ou la télé ?* in two sentences.
9. A friend says *J'adore les maths.* Disagree, and give a reason.

Every reason needs **c'est** or another verb after *parce que*.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Keep the article.** *J'aime **le** sport, je déteste **les** légumes.* Dropping it is an English habit, and it is the error examiners see most in this topic. After *aimer* the article is always the definite one — never *du* or *un*.

**Infinitive after an opinion verb, always.** *J'aime **jouer**, je préfère **regarder**.* If you find yourself writing *j'aime je joue*, stop: only the first verb is conjugated.

**Parce que needs a verb.** *Parce que c'est difficile*, not *parce que difficile*. And before a vowel it is **parce qu'** — *parce qu'il est*. A missing verb after *parce que* is a grammar error, not a spelling one.

**Grade the adjective.** *Très, trop, assez, vraiment* in front of it. *C'est **assez** intéressant mais **trop** long* shows two grades in one sentence, which is range.

**Contrast for free marks.** *Par contre* or *mais* joins two opposite opinions, and two opinions with two reasons is twice the content of one. *J'adore le foot parce que c'est passionnant; par contre, je déteste le rugby parce que c'est dangereux.*

**Use préférer … à.** *Je préfère le tennis **au** foot.* The *à* contracts with *le* to **au**, and the comparison is built into the verb. It is a top-band structure in five words.

**Match the answer to the question.** *Qu'est-ce que tu aimes **faire*** wants an **infinitive**; *tu aimes **le sport*** wants a noun. Answering the wrong shape is a comprehension error as much as a grammar one.

**Vary the verb.** Beyond the ladder: *je m'intéresse à* (I'm interested in), *ça me plaît* (I like it), *je trouve ça génial* (I find it great), *je ne supporte pas* (I can't stand). Three different opinion verbs in a piece of writing is what a Level 4 looks like.

props.title: The first row is the commonest error in Year 9 writing

visuals.alt: A table of common errors in French opinions and the forms that earn marks instead

steps.title: Summary
steps.body: - The ladder: **j'adore** → **j'aime beaucoup** → **j'aime** → **je n'aime pas** → **je déteste**. - With a **noun**, keep the article: *j'aime **le** sport*. - With a **verb**, use the **infinitive**: *j'aime **jouer***. - **Préférer** adds a comparison: *je préfère le tennis **au** foot*. - **Parce que** + a full clause: *parce que **c'est** amusant*. - **Parce qu'** before a vowel. - Grade adjectives with **très, trop, assez, vraiment**. - Negatives wrap the first verb: *je n'aime **pas** …* - Contrast with **par contre** or **mais** for two opinions. - *Tu aimes … ?* → noun; *tu aimes faire … ?* → infinitive. - Agree or disagree: *moi aussi, moi non plus, pas moi, je (ne) suis (pas) d'accord*. - **Aimer** is a regular **-er** verb: *j'aime, tu aimes, il aime, nous aimons, vous aimez, ils aiment*. - Extra opinion verbs: *ça me plaît, je m'intéresse à, je trouve ça …* - An opinion **without a reason** scores little. - Every sentence needs a verb; every noun needs its article.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): single opinions with no reasons, articles often missing
Level 2 (3 to 5): opinions with parce que and c'est, articles mostly kept, one negative
Level 3 (6 to 8): infinitives correct after opinion verbs, graded adjectives, a contrast with par contre
Level 4 (9 to 10): three or more different opinion verbs, préférer … à, a comparison, and reasons that go beyond c'est + adjective

examTechnique.body:
Keep the **article** after an opinion verb and put a second verb in the **infinitive**. Follow *parce que* with **c'est** or another verb, and elide it to *parce qu'* before a vowel.

Grade with **trop / assez / vraiment**, contrast with **par contre**, and answer *aimes faire ?* with an infinitive. An opinion without a reason is only half an answer.
examinerErrors: Dropping the article after aimer, adorer or détester.
Conjugating the second verb instead of using the infinitive.
Writing parce que with no verb after it.
Forgetting to elide parce que before a vowel.
Giving an opinion with no reason.
Using only one opinion verb throughout.
Answering aimes faire with a noun.
Putting pas in the wrong place in a negative.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer keeps every **article** and every **infinitive** right without thinking about it, and never writes *parce que* without a clause. It grades its adjectives — **assez** here, **trop** there — and joins two contrasting opinions with **par contre**. It uses **préférer … à** to build a comparison in five words and reaches beyond *aimer* to **ça me plaît**, **je trouve ça** and **je m'intéresse à**. It reads the shape of the question and answers *aimes faire* with an infinitive, and every opinion it gives comes with a reason.
